Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” said Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1

RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

“They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”

First-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, said Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

“It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”

The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

The funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin said. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2

RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”

“Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”

The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

“The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased new software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”

The Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a new media kit, which Olson said has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.)

The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr said. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” said Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3

The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” said Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”

The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.)

Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”

EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz said. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”

“At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she said, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”

Beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

“I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”

Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”

NotiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

In Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

For instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer said, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

Planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak said. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

“The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak said. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”

Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

The coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants said the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4

This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear plan. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he said it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”

In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin said 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar said, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

So several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

Since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition says it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

When Press Forward first announced the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”

“Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”

The argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”

Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

“I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he said. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”)

Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak said the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”

As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”

LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he said, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”

A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”

The Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

“I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”

The Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”

Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”

“We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”

Does ADHD Worsen With Age? It Depends.

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first became meaningful to how sensitive one’s ADHD is to their environment.

Not too long ago, ADHD was largely thought of as a childhood condition that diminished in adulthood. Today, we understand that ADHD is a lifelong condition. What’s less clear: How does ADHD change across the lifespan, if at all?

This is a question that professor and clinical psychologist Margaret Sibley, Ph.D., addressed during her ADDitude webinar, “How ADHD Symptoms & Impairments Change with Age.”

The answer is still coming into focus but one central truth is emerging: There isn’t a single ADHD experience. Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first become meaningful to how sensitive the individual’s ADHD is to their environment.

Sibley’s take-home from the research? “It depends on who you are.”

The question of how ADHD changes over time — whether it gets better or worse for people — is tricky, in part, because of the symptom vs. impairment question. That is, someone may show symptoms of ADHD, but the degree to which those symptoms impact their life may shift with age, overall health, and myriad other circumstances.

[Your Free Guide to ADHD in Older Adults]

“Not everyone who has symptoms is impaired,” Sibley said.

From major life transitions (like perimenopause and its accompanying impacts on cognition), environmental demands (e.g., a job that strains executive functioning) to coping skills, what’s going on in someone’s life “may influence whether a person actually experiences problems because of their symptoms,” Sibley said.

The question of whether ADHD worsens or improves over time suggests that the condition is linear. For many people, this is not the case.

“It doesn’t get better or get worse. But depending on what’s happening in your life, you may have good years and not-good years,” Sibley said, whose research found that higher environmental demands are associated with “better-functioning ADHD.”

[Read: ADHD’s Vanishing and Reappearing Act]

If you’ve experienced symptoms and impairments since childhood, your symptoms will likely get better, while impairments may or may not worsen.

If your symptoms first began to impact you in adulthood — perhaps triggered by aging, hormonal fluctuations, or other changes — research suggests that your symptoms and impairments may worsen over time.

If you’re part of the subgroup of people whose ADHD fluctuates from year to year, you may have a form of ADHD that is environmentally sensitive.

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

Only 32% of Americans have high confidence that news orgs will report midterm election results accurately, survey finds

About six in 10 Americans said they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents said journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Hate Crimes in Deadly Attack on Boulder, Colorado, Gathering

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

The Frankenstein Table

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

For example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

On the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

But there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically,

is not a presentational element like a
. It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read
I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like

and , they don’t bring in the connection that

and have, and it’s better to reserve
and
for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

So, is it okay if I use

this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):

To me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

But it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

Interesting concept. I like the idea of building out a data/stats card (say, one you’d see in the header of a CRUD edit/view page) with this method.

yes this is indeed scary and i would not use it for these reasons:

– headings are more appropriate in this layout (slap a list or group on it if you want to be more verbose) – changing the display alone already stripped the soul (semantic) of the table – pseudo-semantic is only a developer convenience, not for the end users (VoiceOver is only one of many screen readers, not enough to confirm it works like a real table)

I would suggest a “ in your example. Also the bank does not have a label, correct would be `IssuerName of the bank`. So most of the time there are other ways before using a table with all its markup.

Ha! HTML elements got stripped. So I meant a definition list (dl) and the “Issuer” would be the “th” and “Name of the bank” would be the “td”.

You don’t need to resort to misusing HTML tables for this layout. Your original HTML version could be much improved by simply using sections, headings and paragraphs. In addition, you can also hand over the all-caps and line-breaks styling to CSS while you’re at it. No divs, spans, nor incorrect use of the strong element.

The pseudo-semantic angle is what really sold me here. I run an informational niche site that’s full of reference tables (status codes, payment schedules), and scanning raw markup with / pairs is so much easier to read than a pile of nested divs. That said, Mike Mai’s point about VoiceOver gives me pause — I’ll probably keep this trick for decorative layouts and leave the actual data tables semantically intact.

This is a fun experiment, and I especially liked the distinction you drew between a real table and a pseudo-semantic one. Once display: grid is applied, the browser no longer treats the th and td relationship the way it does in a normal table, so the visual connection stays for sighted readers while the structural meaning is lost. That trade-off is what makes Mike Mai’s point land for me: it is convenient for the author, but assistive technology does not get the same benefit. I would keep this pattern for a purely presentational card only where the same information is also available in a straightforward, accessible form, rather than using it for actual data.

The Ongoing Crisis in Menopause Care

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

Few medical providers are adequately trained to treat menopause, a new study finds, and even fewer understand how hormonal changes aggravate ADHD symptoms.

Suffering through menopausal hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood shifts, and memory problems? Wondering why your ADHD medication has suddenly become less effective? Considering a visit with your doctor to better understand and treat these deeply disruptive symptoms?

Sadly, your healthcare provider may be less informed than you might hope.

A disturbing but unsurprising analysis, published recently in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health, found that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate this often-challenging stage of life. It cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”1

The analysis of 89 studies on health system responsiveness across the U.S. and several other countries also found that women in marginalized groups disproportionately experienced barriers to care and received limited information about available treatment options by providers.

A woman who has gone 12 months without a menstrual period is in menopause. The median age for menopause is 51, though many women with ADHD are known to experience the onset earlier.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

Declining estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause are associated with reduced dopamine, leading to worsening ADHD symptoms and emotional dysregulation in many women – even those who had previously managed their ADHD symptoms well with medication, according to a separate study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.

In surveys conducted over recent years, thousands of women have disclosed to ADDitude how midlife hormonal changes exacerbated their ADHD symptoms and adversely affected every area of their lives, from work performance and sleep to relationships with family and friends. Many said they sought help from providers who had limited knowledge and few clinical studies to consult.

“Perimenopause and menopause play a big role in my inattentive ADHD, and I wish more was known by those who diagnose and treat us,” said Cindy, a ADDitude reader from Santa Clara, California.

“The fact that females are massively underdiagnosed and understudies is horrible but not surprising,” said another ADDitude reader who was diagnosed with ADHD at age 38. “How symptoms may change during perimenopause and menopause, how this affects your home life as a wife and mother, is not talked about enough.”

“It’s insane,” said another ADDitude reader, “and nobody is helping us to treat the super storm of symptoms, including brain fog, exhaustion, headaches, and so on.”

Menopausal hormone therapy is considered the most effective treatment for alleviating common symptoms and is often recommended for women experiencing adverse effects of perimenopause. Non-hormonal medications and complementary approaches, including cognitive behavioral therapy, have also shown benefits in symptom management, the Lancet analysis said.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.

Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

📅 2026-10-29  |  Read Source →

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

The First-Time Experiences Kids Will Never Forget in Citrus County

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

There’s something magical about watching your child experience something for the very first time. The wide eyes. The nervous excitement. The inevitable “Can we do that again?” And the stories they tell anyone who will listen long after you’ve unpacked the suitcases. In Citrus County, Florida, those moments are practically everywhere.

Welcome to Crystal River, Homosassa, Inverness and Floral City—a refreshingly wild side of the Sunshine State where first-time adventures come naturally. Here, kids can swim alongside gentle manatees, search the Gulf for their own dinner, explore underwater worlds and discover that sometimes the best adventures don’t require a screen, a schedule or even a ticket. It’s outdoorsy without requiring your family to be expert adventurers, educational without feeling like school and relaxed enough that you don’t need a vacation from your vacation.

An easy road trip from many Florida cities and an unexpected nature escape for families traveling from farther away, Citrus County is where your next family vacation can become a collection of unforgettable firsts.

Imagine the look on your child’s face when a 1,000-pound manatee glides through the water nearby. It’s the kind of moment that makes even the too-cool-for-everything tween forget to play it cool.

Crystal River is known as the Manatee Capital of the World, and it’s one of the few places in North America where families can swim with these gentle giants in their natural habitat. Book a certified tour with an outfitter like Explorida, where guides teach families the importance of respectful wildlife viewing, including the all-important “Manatee Manners.” Tours operate year-round, but winter is prime time for seeing larger numbers of manatees as they gather in the area’s warm springs.

Not ready to snorkel? Explorida also offers manatee-viewing eco cruises, so younger kids, grandparents and anyone who prefers staying dry can still experience the magic.

Why they’ll remember it: Because seeing a manatee in a book or aquarium is one thing. Sharing the water with one in the wild? That’s a story they’ll be telling for years.

For little explorers (and grandparents) who aren’t ready to jump into the water, the next best thing might be watching nature unfold right beneath their feet.

At Three Sisters Springs, a boardwalk winds around the crystal-clear spring complex, offering an incredible vantage point for spotting manatees during the winter months. The surrounding wetlands are also home to birds and other wildlife, turning an ordinary walk into an impromptu nature safari.

Give your kids a challenge: How many manatees can they spot? Can they find a mother and calf? What other animals can they discover along the way?

It’s stroller-friendly, wonderfully unhurried and proof that you don’t have to get wet to make a splash.

Why they’ll remember it: The thrill of spotting their first wild manatee all on their own, and the pride of being the one who shouts, “I SEE ONE!”

Forget searching for seashells on the beach. In Citrus County, kids can head underwater on a real-life treasure hunt and bring home something delicious.

During summer scalloping season, families venture into the shallow Gulf waters off Crystal River and Homosassa, armed with snorkels, masks and mesh bags, to search the seagrass for bay scallops. Think Easter egg hunt, except underwater. And instead of chocolate, the reward might end up on your dinner plate.

Never tried scalloping? That’s part of the fun. Guided excursions with operators like Explorida help beginners learn the ropes, with equipment, guidance and plenty of encouragement along the way. And the moment your child spots that first scallop hiding in the grass? Pure victory.

Why they’ll remember it: There’s something incredibly satisfying about finding your own food. Just wait until they proudly announce at dinner, “I caught that!”

Tinybeans tip: Scalloping is seasonal, typically July through September. Check current dates, regulations and tour availability before planning your adventure.

For kids who’ve never tried kayaking and paddleboarding, Citrus County offers a pretty spectacular introduction. Imagine pushing off from shore, dipping a paddle into clear spring water and realizing that, for the first time, you’re helping steer the adventure.

At Hunter Springs Park in Crystal River, families will find a freshwater swimming area, kayak launch, waterfront boardwalk, picnic spots and a playground. The spring water stays around 72°F year-round, and during cooler months, there’s even a chance of spotting a manatee.

Bring your own paddle craft or book with a local outfitter. Younger kids can ride along with an adult, while older children can take a more active role in navigating.

The best part? There’s no rush to get anywhere. Stop to watch a bird, look for fish beneath the surface or simply float and take it all in.

Why they’ll remember it: That first feeling of independence. The realization that they can help navigate a kayak, explore somewhere new and discover what’s around the next bend.

What if your kids could explore an underwater world without ever putting on a swimsuit? At Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, they can. The park’s famous Fish Bowl Underwater Observatory lets visitors descend beneath the surface of the spring to watch fish and, when present, manatees swim past the windows. For kids, it’s a little like stepping inside a nature documentary.

Back above water, shady, stroller-accessible boardwalks lead past native Florida wildlife, including black bears, alligators, red wolves and Florida panthers. Daily manatee programs offer another opportunity to learn about these remarkable animals and why protecting their habitat matters.

It’s an ideal first introduction to Florida’s wild side, especially for families with younger children or anyone who prefers wildlife encounters on dry land.

Why they’ll remember it: Because the first time you see the underwater world from a fish’s point of view, you never look at the water quite the same way again.

Remember the first time you rode your bike somewhere that wasn’t your driveway or neighborhood? The freedom. The excitement. The feeling that you could go anywhere? That’s what makes the Withlacoochee State Trail such a great family adventure.

Stretching approximately 47 paved miles through forests, lakes and charming small towns, the trail is flat, scenic and easy to explore in family-sized sections. No one expects your six-year-old to conquer all 47 miles.

Start in downtown Inverness, where the trail passes through the Depot District, and let your kids help choose how far to ride. Along the way, keep an eye out for birds, turtles and other wildlife. When everyone starts asking about snacks, make The Train Station part of your plan for pizza, pretzels and a well-earned break.

Why they’ll remember it: Their first real biking expedition, complete with the satisfaction of going farther than they thought they could. Bonus points if they proudly tell everyone how many miles they conquered.

You can tell your kids mermaids aren’t real. Or you can take them somewhere that might make them question everything.

At Mertailor’s Mermaid Aquarium Encounter in Lecanto, live mermaids perform underwater alongside fish, rays and other marine life, creating a magical experience that feels straight out of a storybook. But there’s more here than mermaid magic. The indoor aquarium features over 20 exhibits, interactive touch tanks, sharks, stingrays and freshwater animals, giving curious kids plenty to explore.

For children ages nine and up, the separate Discover Mermaid experience takes things a step further, with the chance to put on a mermaid tail and monofin and learn to swim like one. It’s also a great rainy-day adventure or a welcome break from the Florida sunshine.

Why they’ll remember it: Because watching a mermaid swim with sharks is pretty unforgettable. But getting to be a mermaid for the first time? That’s next-level vacation bragging rights.

Not every unforgettable first requires an adrenaline rush. Sometimes it’s the first time your kids experience what it feels like to slow down.

Head to Homosassa for a waterfront meal at Crumps’ Landing, where palm trees, water views and laid-back Florida charm set the scene for a different kind of family dinner. No rushing to make a reservation across town. No squeezing in one more attraction. Just good food, waterfront views and time to talk about everything you’ve done together. Let the kids recap their favorite adventures while you watch the sky change colors over the water.

Why they’ll remember it: It may not be the meal they remember years from now, but they’ll remember the feeling: salty air, sunset skies and everyone together with nowhere else they need to be.

Remember when simply staying in a hotel felt like the most exciting thing in the world? Now imagine staying somewhere that puts you right in the middle of the action.

Paddletail Waterfront Lodge sits on King’s Bay in Crystal River, giving families easy access to the area’s most memorable experiences. With paddlecraft activities, manatee excursions, waterfront dining, a pool and complimentary hot breakfast, the lodge makes it easy to spend less time coordinating logistics and more time having fun. Rooms with refrigerators and microwaves, and select kitchenette options also make traveling with kids a little easier.

Wake up knowing that another adventure is waiting just outside.

Why they’ll remember it: Because when the place you stay is part of the experience, even the moments between activities become vacation memories.

Here’s a first that might surprise you: What if you gave your kids an entire afternoon to decide what the family does? No packed itinerary. No racing from one attraction to another. No pressure to squeeze every last minute out of your vacation.

One of the best things about Citrus County is that it gives families room to explore at their own pace. Maybe your kids want another swim at Hunter Springs. Maybe they want to wander downtown Crystal River, go for another bike ride, find ice cream or sit by the water and watch for wildlife. Let them choose.

Because sometimes the most meaningful first isn’t swimming with a manatee or spotting a scallop. It’s the first time your child discovers that an adventure doesn’t need to be planned to be unforgettable.

Why they’ll remember it: Because they helped create the memory themselves. And those are often the moments that stick.

Someday, your kids might forget what they packed, what they ate for breakfast or how long the drive took. But they’ll remember the first manatee they saw. The first scallop they found. The first time they paddled across a spring or rode their bike farther than ever before. And you’ll remember the look on their faces when they did.

That’s the magic of Citrus County. It’s not just a place to visit. It’s a place to try something new, discover something extraordinary and make the kinds of memories that grow more meaningful with time.

Ready to make some first-time memories? Plan your Crystal River and Citrus County getaway and request a FREE Visitor Guide, or book a certified manatee tour and get ready for an adventure your family won’t soon forget.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service

📅 2026-10-28  |  Read Source →

A model can reason about a task. Completing that task takes more: the right context, tools, execution environment, and controls, and an agent loop that brings them together.

Microsoft’s unified harness strategy brings a shared execution foundation across our agent experiences while preserving customer choice. In Microsoft Foundry, that means you can choose a supported model and decide how much of the agent stack to build yourself, without having to assemble every layer around it.

Today, we’re introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service in public preview. It gives developers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. It’s our opinionated approach to helping agents complete complex work. We’re also announcing general availability of long-running resilience for hosted agents. Together, these capabilities help developers build more reliable agents for complex, long-running workflows.

Many teams building agents end up implementing the same execution machinery: coordinating model and tool calls, maintaining working context, managing files, and deciding how to continue when a task requires more than one step. That work matters, but it isn’t usually what differentiates your application.

The Copilot harness gives you a managed execution system for agents you define declaratively in Foundry Agent Service. Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox; you bring the knowledge, procedures, and tools that make the agent yours.

The public preview brings together four building blocks:

The harness manages working context as tasks develop and coordinates model and tool steps toward a requested outcome, within configured limits and policy boundaries. You choose a supported Foundry model without having to rewrite the orchestration around it.

That lets your team focus on improving the agent’s expertise and evaluating its results.

“With the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service, we had a solution running in less than a week, allowing us to focus on design and capabilities instead of the infrastructure underneath it. That speed will help us bring our vision of AI that runs within and alongside our products to market faster.”

— Chris Evans, Chief Technology Officer, Confluence Technologies

“The Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service gives Fashable a powerful foundation for turning complex sourcing processes into governed, measurable agent workflows. We see the opportunity to generate complete tech packs from our knowledge and templates, while extending our A2A sourcing network beyond digitally connected suppliers through email and voice. Most importantly, we can equip brand and manufacturer agents with deeper knowledge and new capabilities to work across sourcing and negotiation without automating away accountability: agents can discover, engage and calculate, while commercially binding decisions remain under human control.”

Consider an agent that researches a topic, analyzes supporting data, and produces an evidence-backed brief. The same pattern can support market research, operational analysis, or an internal planning workflow: instructions define the outcome, skills define the method, and tools provide access to evidence.

Here’s a compact example using the preview Azure Developer CLI (azd) surface.

First, put a reusable procedure in skills/research-brief/SKILL.md:

Then describe the skill and agent in azure.yaml:

Set the referenced environment values, then deploy and invoke:

azd is one authoring option. You can also start in the Foundry portal or use Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code. In the GitHub Copilot app, the Microsoft Foundry plugin and Microsoft Foundry Skill provide a conversational path to creating and managing prompt agents.

These options let you build on a managed harness. When your application needs a different framework or its own execution logic, hosted agents give you another path.

Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service let you bring your own framework, agent loop, middleware, dependencies, and runtime behavior while Foundry manages hosting. Long-running resilience for hosted agents is generally available this week, helping agents recover from interruptions during work that takes hours or days.

Foundry detects interruptions and restarts the work with its original input. Your code saves progress and intermediate results so the agent can pick up where it left off. If the agent updates another system, your workflow also needs to prevent duplicate actions when work restarts.

For example, an agent analyzing a large dataset can save completed stages and resume from the last checkpoint. If it also creates a report in another system, it should check whether the report already exists before creating it again.

Foundry provides the recovery foundation; your application determines what to save and how to resume. Conversation history alone isn’t enough to restore work in progress.

These workflows have different requirements, and there isn’t one right level of abstraction for every agent. Foundry Agent Service lets you choose where to invest your engineering effort:

Start with the level that fits your application’s requirements, rather than taking ownership of infrastructure you don’t need to differentiate.

During this preview, select the Microsoft Copilot harness when creating the agent. Existing agents are unchanged, switching the harness after creation isn’t supported yet, and Foundry manages the execution environment’s CPU, memory, and idle settings.

You can start in the Microsoft Foundry portal or use azd to keep the agent definition alongside the rest of your application.

Pricing: Billing for the Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service begins December 1, 2026, with consumption-based pricing. Harness runtime usage is free before December 1; model inference and separately billed tools and connected services remain subject to their applicable charges. Starting December 1, sandbox compute and memory are billed at USD $0.0994 per vCPU-hour and $0.0118 per GiB-hour, respectively. Prices may vary by region and agreement.

Jeff Hollan is the VP of Product for the Microsoft Foundry Agent Platform.

Viswajeeet is a Principal Software Engineer on Foundry Agents Team in CoreAI, where he leads managed agents platform. He also works on agent identity and toolboxes in Foundry to help customers’ agents achieve better outcomes with right set of controls.

Anthony is a product manager on the Microsoft Foundry team, focused on helping developers build and run AI agents. He works on Foundry Agent Service, making powerful agent capabilities easier to use without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure.
